cls.function: The Surveillance Accountability Act is an amendatory bill that would add section 3119 to title 18, United States Code, and section 1979A to the Revised Statutes.
cls.banner: If enacted, the Surveillance Accountability Act, a proposed bill that is not law, would change existing federal law. It would require a warrant for government searches, including government access to data held by companies, and would let people sue federal officials for violations of Fourth Amendment rights.
cls.checks: All families of checks were run on the Surveillance Accountability Act. Because the bill amends existing law, the analysis looks first at how it fits with the surrounding statutes, their definitions and their remedies.
purpose.ladder.mechanism: The bill would require a warrant before the government conducts a search or accesses data held by third parties, and it would create a cause of action against federal officials.
purpose.ladder.outcome: The intended outcome is that government agencies stop obtaining Americans' personal data without a judge's approval.
purpose.ladder.aim: The ultimate aim of the bill is to end warrantless mass surveillance by the government.
promises.0.p: A press release from Representative Thomas Massie says the bill would create a universal warrant requirement for government searches.
promises.0.why: The bill states the warrant requirement broadly, but it never defines "the government" and it ties the definition of "search" to a court-made test. Several of its definitions reach only searches aimed at a "specific" person, and the bill does not say how it relates to existing surveillance statutes.
promises.1.p: A press release from Representative Lauren Boebert says the bill would cover both federal and local agencies.
promises.1.why: The bill uses "the government" and "a government entity" without saying whether those terms include States and localities. The cause of action in new section 1979A reaches only people acting under federal law.
promises.2.p: The sponsors say in their press releases that the bill would close the third-party doctrine loophole, under which the government obtains data that people have shared with companies without a warrant.
promises.2.why: The bill does contain, in section 3119(a)(2), a direct ban on warrantless government access to third-party data. That ban appears alongside an undefined consent exception, an exception for public information and a definition of "search" built on the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test that produced the third-party doctrine.
promises.3.p: A press release from Representative Lauren Boebert says the bill would ban federal purchases of commercially available location data.
promises.3.why: Section 3119(a)(2)(A) bars warrantless "access" to data held by data brokers, which would cover purchases. The bill does not mention purchase, sale or contractors, and it places no duty on the seller.
promises.4.p: A press release from Representative Thomas Massie says the bill would bar warrantless facial recognition and license plate tracking tied to individuals.
promises.4.why: Section 3119(c) is written as a limit on the exceptions in section 3119(b), not as a prohibition, and its syntax leaves its reach open to more than one reading.
promises.5.p: A press release from Representative Lauren Boebert says the bill would prohibit federal pressure on local law enforcement to share data collected without a warrant.
promises.5.why: No provision of the introduced text addresses data sharing between federal and local agencies or conditions attached to federal grants.
promises.6.p: The sponsors say in their press releases that the bill would let people whose rights are violated sue for damages.
promises.6.why: The cause of action in section 1979A covers rights "secured by the Fourth Amendment", not the new statutory warrant requirement in section 3119. The text is also silent on the immunity defenses that courts apply under the civil rights statute that section 1979A copies.
questions.0.q: The long title of the Surveillance Accountability Act promises warrants for searches that "significantly impinge on the privacy or security of a person". Where does that standard appear in the operative text of the bill?
questions.0.a: That standard does not appear in the operative text. The operative definition of "search" in section 3119(d)(1) uses a different test, a "reasonable expectation of privacy". A court comparing the title with the text would give effect to the text.
questions.1.q: Which governments would be bound when section 3119(a)(2)(A) of the bill says "The government shall not access" third-party data without a warrant?
questions.1.a: The bill does not say. New section 3119 sits in title 18, which governs federal criminal procedure, and the cause of action in section 1979A is limited to people acting under color of federal law. One sponsor's press release says local agencies are covered. If States are meant to be bound, the bill would need to say so and rest on a constitutional power that allows it.
questions.2.q: Who creates, holds, moves, sells and uses the personal data that the Surveillance Accountability Act addresses, and at what point in that sequence does the bill act?
questions.2.a: Apps, carriers, banks and device makers collect the data. Data brokers aggregate and sell it. Agencies and their contractors buy or demand it. The bill acts at one point only, the government's access, and it places no duty on the companies that collect or sell the data.
questions.3.q: Which agencies have obtained personal data held by companies without a warrant before, and on what legal theory?
questions.3.a: After the Supreme Court required a warrant for cell-site location records in 2018, a Defense Intelligence Agency memo disclosed in 2021 said the agency bought commercial smartphone location data and did not read the ruling to require a warrant for purchased data. A declassified 2022 report to the Director of National Intelligence described large-scale purchases of commercially available information across the intelligence community.
questions.4.q: If the Surveillance Accountability Act closes direct warrantless access to personal data, what is the next least costly way for an agency to obtain the same information?
questions.4.a: The text leaves several such ways available. An agency could rely on an existing statute that authorizes collection on a lower standard and argue that this general warrant requirement did not repeal it. It could collect in bulk, since two definitions of "search" reach only searches of a "specific" person. It could query data it already holds, since the data definition speaks of "acquisition and analysis" together. It could rely on someone's "consent". It could treat purchased data as publicly available. It could have a contractor or partner agency hold the data.
questions.5.q: Which existing laws let agencies obtain third-party data on less than a probable-cause warrant, and what does the Surveillance Accountability Act say about them?
questions.5.a: Several laws do, including court orders and subpoenas under the Stored Communications Act, national security letters, foreign intelligence collection under section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, and mandatory financial reporting. The bill mentions none of them and has no clause stating that it overrides other law. Courts disfavor implied repeals and generally let a specific statute govern over a general one.
questions.6.q: If an agency conducts a search without a warrant in violation of new section 3119, what consequence would the Surveillance Accountability Act impose?
questions.6.a: Section 3119 has no remedy of its own. Evidence would not be excluded, because the bill provides no suppression rule. The new cause of action in section 1979A covers Fourth Amendment violations, which may not include conduct that only the statute forbids. An official sued under section 1979A can be expected to raise the immunity defenses that courts apply under the parallel civil rights statute.
questions.7.q: Exception (5) in section 3119(b) allows "searches conducted with consent". Whose consent would satisfy that exception?
questions.7.a: The text does not say. Section 3119(a)(2)(A) provides that a third party's consent cannot substitute for a warrant, and section 3119(a)(2)(B) limits waiver by contract, but the consent exception in section 3119(b)(5) is itself unqualified.
questions.8.q: Who would bear the effects if the Surveillance Accountability Act worked exactly as written?
questions.8.a: People whose data is held by companies would gain a warrant requirement that applies against the government. The same data would still be collected, sold to private buyers and exposed to breach. Investigators would lose tools they use lawfully today, including in fraud, child exploitation and missing-person cases, which is the trade-off critics of the bill raise.
questions.9.q: Would anyone have to report on, audit or count the searches carried out under the Surveillance Accountability Act?
questions.9.a: The bill would not require anyone to do so. It contains no reporting requirement, inspector general role or audit, so Congress and the public would have no routine way to learn whether warrantless access had stopped.
questions.10.q: What is the smallest set of changes to the Surveillance Accountability Act that would make its text match what the sponsors promised?
questions.10.a: The bill would need to define "government", make the cause of action cover violations of section 3119, state how section 3119 relates to existing surveillance statutes, specify whose consent counts, reach bulk collection and data already held, and add a suppression rule. The broader aim of ending the trade in this data would need a separate provision aimed at sellers.
findings.S1.title: The warrant requirement in section 3119 of the Surveillance Accountability Act applies to "the government", a term the bill does not define.
findings.S1.plain: Section 3119 provides that "the government" may not access personal data without a warrant, and the bill never states which governments are covered. The open term could reach every agency at every level of government. It could also be read to mean federal law enforcement only, which would leave state and local agencies outside the requirement.
findings.S1.tech: Section 3119 uses "the government", "government-initiated" and "a government entity or its agents" without definition. Chapter 205 of title 18 governs federal criminal procedure, and new section 1979A reaches only action under color of federal law, both of which point toward a federal-only reading. One sponsor's press release says local agencies are covered. If States are covered, a statutory rule broader than the Fourth Amendment as courts read it would need a constitutional basis for binding them, which invites challenge.
findings.S1.use: A state or local agency could argue that section 3119 does not apply to it. A federal agency could then obtain the same data from a state or local partner agency.
findings.S1.am.S1b.label: Open definition of "government" that names the disputed cases
findings.S1.am.S1b.cost: This option uses "includes", which the House and Senate drafting manuals reserve for a definition that is not exhaustive, so "government" stays open while the definition expressly names intelligence elements, Armed Forces components, States and their political subdivisions, and contractors, covering the three documented gaps. Naming States outright raises the federalism question, which the narrower option avoids.
findings.S1.am.S1a.label: Closed definition of "government" limited to listed entities
findings.S1.am.S1a.cost: A closed definition of "government" gives certainty and loses the breadth of the open term, because any entity not listed is presumed excluded. This version also reaches States only through federal involvement, when they act jointly with, at the request of, or with funds from a federal entity.
findings.S1.inq.q: Which agencies would fall inside or outside the warrant requirement of the Surveillance Accountability Act, depending on what "the government" means?
findings.S1.inq.items.0.h: Florida state officers have run license plate searches on behalf of Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
findings.S1.inq.items.0.d: Audit logs show Florida's wildlife police ran license plate lookups for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with each search querying more than 5,000 camera networks. The federal agency had no contract with the camera company. If "the government" in section 3119 means federal agencies only, the state officers' searches fall outside the warrant requirement.
findings.S1.inq.items.1.h: Border Patrol has searched license plate data collected by local police departments.
findings.S1.inq.items.1.d: University of Washington researchers found that Border Patrol ran hundreds if not thousands of searches of local police license plate data through a nationwide lookup setting. California's attorney general wrote to 20 police departments about federal access to that data and sued one of them.
findings.S1.inq.items.2.h: The Surveillance Accountability Act does not say whether military and intelligence agencies count as "the government".
findings.S1.inq.items.2.d: The disclosed purchases of location data were made by the Defense Intelligence Agency. New section 3119 sits in the criminal procedure title of the United States Code, which governs law enforcement. The text does not say that defense and intelligence components are "the government" for purposes of section 3119.
findings.S1.inq.items.3.h: The cause of action in section 1979A of the Surveillance Accountability Act reaches fewer actors than the warrant requirement in its section 3119.
findings.S1.inq.items.3.d: Section 1979A reaches only persons acting under color of federal law. A state officer who runs a search for a federal agency could be sued, if at all, only under the existing civil rights statute and only for a constitutional violation.
findings.S1.inq.open: No court has interpreted "the government" as used in this bill. Representative Boebert's press release states that local agencies would be covered, and the bill's text does not say so.
findings.S1.two.dec: Which entity would first construe "the government" in the Surveillance Accountability Act, given that the bill names no implementing agency and its cause of action reaches only federal actors?
findings.S1.two.views.0.why: The sponsors would likely support defining "the government", because one sponsor's press release says local agencies are covered and the text does not say so.
findings.S2.title: Section 3119(d)(1) of the Surveillance Accountability Act defines "search" by the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test, from which the third-party doctrine derives.
findings.S2.plain: Section 3119(d)(1) defines a search as an act that intrudes on a "reasonable expectation of privacy". Courts used that same phrase to hold that people have no such expectation in data they share with companies. The bill's long title uses a different standard, searches that "significantly impinge" on privacy, which appears nowhere in the operative text.
findings.S2.tech: The third-party doctrine holds that a person has no reasonable expectation of privacy in information voluntarily conveyed to a third party, and the Supreme Court narrowed it for cell-site location records in 2018 without overruling it. The definition in section 3119(d)(1) lists subparagraphs (A) through (C) after "including the following". It is unclear whether the listed items are searches regardless of the expectation test or only examples that must still satisfy it. Section 3119(a)(2) is drafted as a separate command and does not depend on the definition, which supports its coverage of third-party data. The long title's phrase "significantly impinge on the privacy or security of a person" is a third formulation. Courts may consult a title to resolve ambiguity in the text, so the title gives a party arguing for a narrow reading one more thing to cite.
findings.S2.use: A defendant agency could argue that access to shared data is not a "search" under section 3119(d) because no reasonable expectation of privacy exists. It could cite the long title to argue that only significant intrusions were meant, and argue that section 3119(a)(2) is limited the same way.
findings.S2.am.S2a.label: Make the listed categories of search independent of the expectation-of-privacy test
findings.S2.am.S2a.cost: Amending section 3119(d)(1) so the listed categories apply without regard to the expectation test would, read with subparagraph (C), make nearly any government handling of personal information a search. That breadth would increase the pressure for clear exceptions.
findings.S3.title: Two of the three definitions of "search" in section 3119(d)(1) of the Surveillance Accountability Act are limited to acts directed at a specific person.
findings.S3.plain: Subparagraphs (A) and (B) of section 3119(d)(1) cover only acts aimed at a "specific" person or entity. Collecting data on everyone at once is, by its nature, not aimed at anyone specific.
findings.S3.tech: Section 3119(d)(1)(A) covers acts "purposefully directed at a specific person or entity". Section 3119(d)(1)(B) covers surveillance that "collects information on a specific individual or entity". Only subparagraph (C) lacks the qualifier, and it has its own limit, the conjunctive phrase "acquisition and analysis". Bulk collection is the practice the sponsors describe as the problem.
findings.S3.use: An agency could characterize a program as untargeted bulk acquisition that falls outside section 3119(d)(1)(A) and (B).
findings.S3.am.S3a.label: Add bulk collection to the definition of "search"
findings.S3.am.S3a.cost: Because a warrant must particularly describe what is sought, adding bulk collection to section 3119(d)(1) would in practice bar bulk acquisition, not just regulate it. That is a policy decision with consequences for agencies that analyze aggregate data for non-investigative purposes.
findings.S4.title: The phrase "acquisition and analysis" in the personal-data definition of the Surveillance Accountability Act, section 3119(d)(1)(C), is conjunctive and may be read to require both acts.
findings.S4.plain: Section 3119(d)(1)(C) covers the "acquisition and analysis" of personal data. Read strictly, an agency that queries data it already holds is analyzing without acquiring.
findings.S4.tech: The word "and" is ordinarily conjunctive. Section 3119(c) separately lists "collection, retention, querying, or analysis", which shows the drafters knew how to list the acts disjunctively. Queries of previously collected data are a central issue in the current surveillance debate.
findings.S4.use: An agency could query, without a warrant, data acquired before enactment or acquired lawfully under another authority.
findings.S4.am.S4a.label: List acquisition, retention, querying and analysis separately
findings.S4.am.S4a.cost: Replacing "acquisition and analysis" with a disjunctive list would make retention itself a search, which would require a transition rule for data agencies hold today.
findings.S5.title: The consent exception in section 3119(b)(5) of the Surveillance Accountability Act does not specify whose consent permits a warrantless search.
findings.S5.plain: Under section 3119(b)(5), searches conducted "with consent" require no warrant. The bill does not specify whose consent counts: the person the data concerns, or the company holding it.
findings.S5.tech: Section 3119(a)(2)(A) bars access to third-party data "regardless of whether the third party consents", and section 3119(a)(2)(B) restricts waiver by contract unless it is "knowing, voluntary, and explicit". Section 3119(b), however, is introduced by "The following may be conducted without a warrant", and paragraph (5) is unqualified. Only section 3119(a)(1) is expressly made subject to subsection (b), so the interaction of (b)(5) with (a)(2) is left to inference.
findings.S5.use: A click-through agreement labeled knowing, voluntary and explicit could satisfy section 3119(a)(2)(B), and the government could then claim consent under section 3119(b)(5) for every search that follows.
findings.S5.am.S5a.label: Require the consent of the person searched
findings.S5.am.S5a.cost: Third-party consent has legitimate uses, such as a business reporting a crime against itself using its own records. Limiting section 3119(b)(5) to the consent of the individual searched may therefore require a carve-out for a third party's own business records about its own victimization.
findings.S6.title: The public-information exception in section 3119(b)(3) of the Surveillance Accountability Act does not require that the person the information concerns be the one who made it public.
findings.S6.plain: Under section 3119(b)(3), information "made available by a person or entity to a public audience" requires no warrant. The text does not require that the person the information concerns be the one who made it public.
findings.S6.tech: Section 3119(b)(3) turns on publication "by a person or entity", meaning any person or entity. Agencies have described purchased datasets as commercially or publicly available. Section 3119(c) limits the exceptions for data "exposed to public view or accessible to a third party", but only "with respect to data gathered by entering a public place" and similar settings.
findings.S6.use: An agency could treat a dataset offered for sale to any buyer as made available to a public audience and obtain it without a warrant.
findings.S6.am.S6a.label: Limit the exception to information the individual published
findings.S6.am.S6a.cost: Limiting section 3119(b)(3) to information the individual made public without charge could require a warrant to read a news article about someone. Section 3119(b)(4), which covers news outlets and public records, would then have to cover that use and should be reviewed alongside the change.
findings.S8.title: Section 3119(c) of the Surveillance Accountability Act, on facial recognition and license plate readers, is syntactically ambiguous and may be read to protect less than the sponsors describe.
findings.S8.plain: The sentence in section 3119(c) meant to protect people from facial recognition and license plate tracking is a single long clause with several conditions. It can be read to cover much less than the sponsors describe.
findings.S8.tech: Section 3119(c) is a rule of construction for the exceptions in section 3119(b), not a prohibition. It applies only where "the person associated with the collected identifiers" did not consent. The full condition reads "did not express informed and voluntary consent to such collection with respect to data gathered by entering a public place, operating a motor vehicle on a public roadway, or patronizing a private establishment open to the public". The trailing phrase beginning "with respect to" can modify the consent requirement or the whole limitation. The two listed data types follow "including", which leaves open whether other data is covered.
findings.S8.use: An agency could argue that data gathered in a setting not listed in section 3119(c), such as an online platform, is outside the limitation.
findings.S8.am.S8a.label: Restate section 3119(c) as a direct prohibition
findings.S8.am.S8a.cost: A flat prohibition on warrantless collection of biometric and license plate data would reach ordinary uses such as checking a plate during a traffic stop. Exception (2) in section 3119(b) covers identity documents but not license plates, so the traffic-stop plate check would need its own treatment.
findings.S9.title: The savings clause in section 3119(e)(3) of the Surveillance Accountability Act preserves searches incident to "ordinary" law enforcement encounters without defining what makes an encounter ordinary.
findings.S9.plain: Section 3119(e)(3) provides that nothing in section 3119 restricts searches "incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters". It does not state what makes an encounter ordinary.
findings.S9.tech: Section 3119(e)(3) preserves authority to conduct detentions, frisks, arrests "or searches incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters". The familiar doctrine is search incident to arrest. A search "incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters" is a broader and undefined category, and a rule of construction that preserves existing authority can be argued to override the new warrant requirement wherever the two meet.
findings.S9.use: A search of an electronic device during a routine stop could be defended as incident to an ordinary law enforcement encounter.
findings.S9.am.S9a.label: Limit the savings clause to searches incident to a lawful arrest
findings.S9.am.S9a.cost: Limiting section 3119(e)(3) to searches of the person incident to a lawful arrest, excluding device contents, would be narrower than current practice in some settings, and law enforcement groups would object.
findings.S10.title: The Surveillance Accountability Act's cause of action in section 1979A covers Fourth Amendment violations but not violations of the bill's statutory warrant requirement in section 3119.
findings.S10.plain: The bill creates a new warrant requirement in section 3119 and a cause of action in section 1979A. The cause of action covers violations of the Fourth Amendment, not violations of section 3119. Where section 3119 goes further than courts say the Constitution does, there may be no claim to bring.
findings.S10.tech: Section 1979A creates liability for deprivation of rights "secured by the Fourth Amendment". Section 3119 is a statute whose purpose is to require warrants in situations, such as third-party data, where current doctrine says the Fourth Amendment does not. A violation of section 3119 that is not also a constitutional violation falls outside section 1979A, and section 3119 has no remedy clause of its own.
findings.S10.use: An agency could concede a violation of section 3119 and still win dismissal because no constitutional right was infringed.
findings.S10.am.S10a.label: Extend the cause of action to violations of section 3119
findings.S10.am.S10a.cost: Extending section 1979A to violations of section 3119 would expand personal liability for federal employees to a new and untested statutory standard. That change would likely bring pressure to add a good-faith defense, which raises the separate qualified immunity issue.
findings.S10.inq.q: Which practices targeted by the Surveillance Accountability Act would violate section 3119 but not the Fourth Amendment as courts now read it?
findings.S10.inq.items.0.h: Warrantless access to bank and financial records would violate section 3119 of the Surveillance Accountability Act but not the Fourth Amendment.
findings.S10.inq.items.0.d: The Supreme Court held in 1976 that a customer has no Fourth Amendment interest in records held by a bank. The 2018 Carpenter decision said it did not disturb that holding. Warrantless access to bank records would breach new section 3119 and still not be a deprivation of a right "secured by the Fourth Amendment".
findings.S10.inq.items.1.h: Warrantless access to phone and internet metadata would violate section 3119 of the Surveillance Accountability Act but not the Fourth Amendment.
findings.S10.inq.items.1.d: The same is true of numbers dialed and similar records under the Supreme Court's 1979 decision, which Carpenter also left in place.
findings.S10.inq.items.2.h: The Supreme Court has not decided whether data the government buys from data brokers is protected by the Fourth Amendment.
findings.S10.inq.items.2.d: The Supreme Court has not ruled on purchased data. At least one agency has taken the position that the 2018 ruling does not require a warrant for it.
findings.S10.inq.items.3.h: The Supreme Court has not held that facial recognition or license plate readers in public are Fourth Amendment searches.
findings.S10.inq.items.3.d: The Supreme Court has not held that either practice is a search. Section 3119(c) attempts to protect against both, and the cause of action in section 1979A would not follow.
findings.S10.inq.open: Lower courts differ on some of these practices. The conclusion that section 1979A does not reach a violation of section 3119 holds wherever a court finds no constitutional search.
findings.S12.title: The Surveillance Accountability Act's attorney's fees provision in section 1979A(b) refers to "this Act", although that text would be inserted into the Revised Statutes.
findings.S12.plain: Section 1979A(b) allows attorney's fees in suits "to enforce this Act". Because that subsection would be inserted into the Revised Statutes, an old compilation of laws, "this Act" has no clear referent there.
findings.S12.tech: Section 1979A(b) would be new text of the Revised Statutes. Inside inserted text, "this Act" would ordinarily be read as the statute being amended, not the Surveillance Accountability Act. The parallel fee provision for civil rights suits refers to the relevant sections by number.
findings.S12.use: A party opposing a fee award could contest it on the ground that the suit enforces a section of the Revised Statutes, not an Act.
findings.S12.am.S12a.label: Refer to "this section" in section 1979A(b)
findings.S12.am.S12a.cost: Replacing "this Act" with "this section" in section 1979A(b) has no identified cost.
findings.S13.title: The introduced text of the Surveillance Accountability Act contains four drafting errors, one of them in an exception to the warrant requirement.
findings.S13.plain: The text misspells "Definitions", says "Searched conducted" where it means "Searches conducted", says "new outlets" where it means "news outlets", and leaves the word "is" out of the amending instruction in section 2(b).
findings.S13.tech: Three of the errors are harmless. The phrase "new outlets" in the exception in section 3119(b)(4) could be argued to mean something other than news organizations. The clerical amendment, which reads "United States Code, amended by adding", lacks an operative verb.
findings.S13.use: The practical effect of the drafting errors is minimal, but errors in an exception clause are the kind that get litigated.
findings.S13.am.S13a.label: Correct all four drafting errors
findings.S13.am.S13a.cost: Correcting the four drafting errors has no identified cost.
findings.S15.title: Read literally, the Surveillance Accountability Act's ban in section 3119(a)(2)(A) on warrantless access to third-party data extends to routine regulatory reporting by banks and employers.
findings.S15.plain: Section 3119(a)(2)(A) covers "any data" held by a third party. Read literally, that includes records agencies collect every day outside the surveillance context, such as reports that banks and employers are required to file.
findings.S15.tech: Section 3119(a)(2)(A) is not limited to data about individuals, to investigations, or to compelled or purchased access. Mandatory reporting schemes, regulatory inspections and civil subpoenas all involve the government accessing data held by third parties. Courts faced with a rule this broad and no override clause tend to read it narrowly to avoid upending other statutes, and the narrowing can cut into the intended coverage.
findings.S15.use: The breadth of section 3119(a)(2)(A) could become the argument for reading it narrowly across the board.
findings.S15.am.S15a.label: Limit the ban to personal data sought for investigation or intelligence
findings.S15.am.S15a.cost: A purpose limit in section 3119(a)(2)(A) creates its own gap, because data gathered for an administrative purpose can later be shared with investigators. A use restriction would be needed alongside it.
findings.S7.title: The exigent-circumstances exception in section 3119(b)(6) of the Surveillance Accountability Act is undefined and requires no after-the-fact review of warrantless emergency searches.
findings.S7.plain: Section 3119(b)(6) exempts searches conducted under exigent circumstances from the warrant requirement. The bill does not define an emergency or require anyone to review an emergency claim afterward.
findings.S7.tech: Leaving "exigent circumstances" undefined imports existing doctrine, which is a reasonable drafting choice. Other surveillance statutes that allow emergency access pair it with after-the-fact court approval within a fixed time.
findings.S7.use: Warrantless emergency access could become routine where no one reviews it.
findings.S11.title: The Surveillance Accountability Act's cause of action in section 1979A does not address whether qualified immunity is available to federal officials sued under it.
findings.S11.plain: Section 1979A copies the wording of the main civil rights statute. Courts allow officials sued under that statute to avoid damages unless the right was already clearly established. The bill does not say whether the same defense applies to suits under section 1979A.
findings.S11.tech: Section 1979A(a) tracks section 1979 of the Revised Statutes, which is section 1983 of title 42, United States Code. Qualified immunity under that statute is a judicial doctrine, and a court would likely carry it over to parallel text absent a contrary instruction. For new surveillance technologies, the law is rarely clearly established. The Supreme Court has also sharply limited court-created damages suits against federal officers, which is why a statutory action matters and why its details do.
findings.S11.use: Damages claims under section 1979A could fail at the outset on immunity grounds even where a violation occurred.
findings.S11.am.S11a.label: Address qualified immunity and set minimum damages
findings.S11.am.S11a.cost: Removing qualified immunity for federal employees is contested and would draw opposition from law enforcement and national security agencies. An alternative is to make the United States, not the individual official, the liable party.
findings.S16.title: The Surveillance Accountability Act contains no exclusionary rule for evidence obtained in violation of the warrant requirement in section 3119.
findings.S16.plain: The bill does not provide that evidence obtained without a warrant required by section 3119 must be excluded from court. Without such a rule, the main everyday check on unlawful searches is absent for any protection the bill adds beyond the Constitution.
findings.S16.tech: Suppression is a constitutional remedy. For purely statutory violations, courts generally do not exclude evidence unless the statute says so, as the federal wiretap law does.
findings.S16.use: Data obtained in violation of section 3119 could be used in prosecutions and other proceedings.
findings.S16.am.S16a.label: Add an exclusionary rule for violations of section 3119
findings.S16.am.S16a.cost: An exclusionary rule could end prosecutions over drafting ambiguities elsewhere in the bill, which raises the stakes of every other drafting issue identified in this analysis.
findings.S17.title: The Surveillance Accountability Act does not state how section 3119 interacts with existing statutes that authorize collection without a probable-cause warrant.
findings.S17.plain: Several existing statutes, including foreign intelligence law, let agencies obtain data without a probable-cause warrant. The bill does not mention them or state that section 3119 controls if they conflict.
findings.S17.tech: The bill contains no statement of how section 3119 relates to other law and no conforming amendment to the Stored Communications Act, the national security letter statutes, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act or financial reporting laws. Implied repeals are disfavored, and a specific statute ordinarily controls over a general one. Section 3119(e)(1) says the section does not "authorize surveillance that would otherwise be unlawful" but is silent on surveillance that is otherwise lawful. The Senate drafting manual advises against a general "notwithstanding any other provision of law" clause, on the ground that it is unlikely to have effect, and tells drafters to identify and cite the conflicting law.
findings.S17.use: An agency could continue to use a specific existing authority and argue that the general warrant requirement in section 3119 left it intact. This is the most direct route around the bill for intelligence agencies.
findings.S17.am.S17a.label: Name the statutes that section 3119 overrides
findings.S17.am.S17a.cost: This option cites each affected law by name, as the Senate drafting manual advises, in place of a general override. Any authority not named survives, so the list has to be complete, and financial reporting law and administrative subpoenas are left out of this version and would continue. It would restructure intelligence collection that touches Americans and would send the bill to additional committees.
findings.S17.inq.q: Which specific existing authorities let federal agencies obtain data covered by section 3119 on less than a probable-cause warrant?
findings.S17.inq.items.0.h: Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act permits foreign intelligence collection without individual warrants.
findings.S17.inq.items.0.d: Section 702 collection covered nearly 250,000 targets in 2022, approved by annual court certification and not by individual warrants. The FBI ran roughly 119,000 searches of the collected data using Americans' identifiers that year.
findings.S17.inq.items.1.h: The Stored Communications Act lets courts order disclosure of records on less than probable cause.
findings.S17.inq.items.1.d: Section 2703(d) of title 18, United States Code, lets a court order disclosure of records on "specific and articulable facts", a lower standard than probable cause.
findings.S17.inq.items.2.h: National security letters let the FBI demand records without a judge.
findings.S17.inq.items.2.d: Section 2709 of title 18, United States Code, lets the FBI demand subscriber and transaction records on its own certification, with no judge involved.
findings.S17.inq.items.3.h: Federal law requires banks to report suspicious activity to the Treasury Department without any warrant.
findings.S17.inq.items.3.d: Section 5318(g) of title 31, United States Code, requires banks to file suspicious activity reports with the Treasury Department. The government receives financial data about named individuals with no warrant and no request.
findings.S17.inq.items.4.h: Administrative subpoenas let agencies demand business records without going to a court.
findings.S17.inq.items.4.d: Dozens of statutes let agencies subpoena business records without a court, for example section 876 of title 21, United States Code, for drug investigations.
findings.S17.inq.items.5.h: Executive Order 12333 governs intelligence collection abroad under presidential authority.
findings.S17.inq.items.5.d: Intelligence collection abroad proceeds under presidential authority, not statute. The Surveillance Accountability Act, a general amendment to title 18, does not mention Executive Order 12333.
findings.S17.inq.open: The statute citations in this list are given so they can be checked, and the cited sections themselves were not opened in this review. The 2022 figures are the most recent that were verified.
findings.S17.two.dec: Is the Surveillance Accountability Act intended to alter intelligence collection, or only law enforcement practice?
findings.S17.two.views.0.why: Intelligence and counterterrorism officials would favor the bill's silence, because silence leaves existing intelligence authorities standing.
findings.S17.two.views.1.why: Members of Congress who favor renewing existing surveillance law first would rather reauthorize current law and take up reform afterward.
findings.S17.two.views.2.why: A coalition of privacy and civil liberties groups has asked for a warrant requirement on queries of intelligence data and for the data broker loophole to be closed.
findings.S18.title: The Surveillance Accountability Act specifies no effective date and no rule for personal data already in agency possession.
findings.S18.plain: The bill does not state when it would take effect or what would happen to data agencies already hold.
findings.S18.tech: Without an effective date, the Act would take effect on enactment. The bill contains no provision on retention, deletion or continued querying of data acquired earlier, and no treatment of pending investigations.
findings.S18.use: Agencies could continue to use existing datasets after enactment.
findings.S19.title: The Surveillance Accountability Act imposes no reporting, audit or inspector general requirement on agencies subject to the warrant requirement.
findings.S19.plain: The bill contains no reporting requirement, audit or inspector general role. There would be no regular means of knowing whether agencies had stopped warrantless access.
findings.S19.tech: Surveillance statutes commonly require annual reports of orders sought and granted and periodic inspector general review. The cause of action depends on people learning they were searched, and the bill has no notice requirement.
findings.S19.use: Violations of section 3119 that are never disclosed could never be challenged.
findings.S21.title: A provision a sponsor's press release describes, on federal pressure on local police to share locally collected data, is absent from the introduced Surveillance Accountability Act.
findings.S21.plain: One sponsor's press release says the bill would stop federal agencies from pressuring local police to share surveillance data. No such provision appears in the introduced text.
findings.S21.tech: The press release lists a prohibition on federal pressure on local law enforcement to share warrantlessly collected data. The introduced text contains no provision on intergovernmental sharing, grant conditions or fusion centers. The provision may have appeared in an earlier draft.
findings.S21.use: Readers relying on the sponsor's press release could believe the bill addresses federal pressure on local police to share data.
findings.S20.title: The Surveillance Accountability Act restricts government acquisition of data from data brokers and does not regulate the brokers' collection or sale of that data.
findings.S20.plain: Section 3119(a)(2)(A) bars the government from accessing brokered data without a warrant. It does not stop companies from collecting that data or selling it. The data would continue to exist, and any gap in the government-side restriction would leave it within reach.
findings.S20.tech: Disclosed practice shows the significance of this design. A Defense Intelligence Agency memo disclosed in 2021 described purchases of commercial location data, and a declassified 2022 report described intelligence community purchases of commercially available information at scale. Supply-side designs already exist elsewhere. Montana in 2025 barred its own agencies from buying such data, and the House in 2024 passed a bill aimed at government purchases from brokers. None of these ends the collection itself.
findings.S20.use: Any agency or partner outside the reach of section 3119 could still purchase the data.
findings.S20.am.S20a.label: Broader option: regulate data brokers as sellers
findings.S20.am.S20a.cost: This option goes beyond the bill's stated purpose. Restrictions on selling information face First Amendment challenges, "data broker" would need a definition, and companies that collect data directly are not brokers. Prohibiting the brokerage business altogether would be a further step with larger economic effects and the same gap for first-party collectors.
findings.S20.two.dec: Is the Surveillance Accountability Act intended to constrain government acquisition of personal data, or to end the commercial trade in that data?
findings.S20.two.views.0.why: Data brokers and advertising technology firms would prefer a rule aimed only at the government buyer, which leaves their business intact.
bigger.issue: Fourth Amendment protection of personal data in the digital age
bigger.lead: Even if every provision of the Surveillance Accountability Act worked as intended, the bill would impose a warrant requirement on government access to data. For the reasons below, it would not by itself end warrantless surveillance.
bigger.map.0.part: Government access to personal data held by companies
bigger.map.0.note: Government access to data held by companies is the core of new section 3119(a)(2).
bigger.map.1.part: Government purchases of personal data from data brokers
bigger.map.1.note: Section 3119(a)(2) covers purchases from data brokers as "access", but it does not name purchase or contractors.
bigger.map.2.part: Collection and sale of personal data by private companies
bigger.map.2.note: The bill places no duty on collectors or sellers. The data remains available to other buyers, including foreign ones.
bigger.map.3.part: Foreign intelligence collection that acquires Americans' data
bigger.map.3.note: Foreign intelligence collection is governed by separate statutes and executive authority that the bill does not mention.
bigger.map.4.part: Existing lower-standard court orders, subpoenas and national security letters
bigger.map.4.note: The bill contains no override clause and no conforming amendments for these existing authorities.
bigger.map.5.note: Coverage of state and local surveillance depends on the undefined term "the government".
bigger.map.6.part: Government-run sensors: facial recognition and license plate readers
bigger.map.6.note: The bill addresses these sensors through section 3119(c), a limit on the exceptions whose reach is uncertain.
bigger.map.7.part: Personal data that agencies already hold
bigger.map.7.note: The bill sets no retention, deletion or query rule for existing datasets.
bigger.map.8.part: Remedies when the warrant requirement is violated
bigger.map.8.note: The bill provides a cause of action for constitutional violations only, includes no suppression rule and does not address immunity.
bigger.map.9.part: Transparency and oversight of government searches
bigger.map.9.note: The bill requires no reporting, no audit and no notice to people who were searched.
stake.priv.want: Privacy and civil liberties advocates want a warrant requirement with no gaps and an end to government purchases from data brokers.
stake.fle.want: Federal criminal investigators want fast lawful access to records in fraud, trafficking and missing-person cases. Critics of the bill say warrant requirements slow investigations.
stake.ic.want: Intelligence and counterterrorism officials want existing foreign intelligence authorities left intact.
stake.slp.want: State and local police want continued use of license plate readers and shared databases, and a clear answer on whether the warrant requirement binds them.
stake.brok.role: Data brokers and advertising technology firms
stake.brok.want: Data brokers and advertising technology firms want to keep selling personal data, with the government as one customer among many.
stake.hold.want: Companies that hold customer data want a clear rule on when they must hand data over to the government, and no liability for following it.
stake.surv.want: People most exposed to surveillance want protection that does not depend on which agency is collecting their data. Reporting shows local camera data reaching immigration enforcement.
stake.vict.want: Crime victims and their advocates want investigations that are not slowed when someone is in danger.
stake.spon.role: Sponsors of the Surveillance Accountability Act
stake.spon.want: The bill's sponsors want a warrant for every government search and describe the bill as covering federal and local agencies.
stake.opp.role: Members of Congress who favor renewing existing surveillance law first
stake.opp.want: Members of Congress who favor renewing existing surveillance law first want current authorities reauthorized, with wider reform left for later.
stake.pl.role: Civil rights lawyers who would bring suits under the bill
stake.pl.want: Civil rights lawyers who would bring suits under the bill want a cause of action that survives a motion to dismiss.
stake.def.role: Government lawyers who would defend those suits
stake.def.want: Government lawyers who would defend suits under the bill want the narrowest defensible reading of each duty it creates.
stake.tex.role: A judge who reads statutes by their text
stake.tex.want: A judge who reads statutes by their text applies the words as written and will not supply what Congress left out.
stake.pur.role: A judge who reads statutes by their purpose
stake.pur.want: A judge who reads statutes by their purpose resolves doubt in favor of what the law was trying to do.
stake.olc.want: A legislative drafter wants every key term defined, every cross-reference checked and every relationship to existing law stated.
findings.S22.title: Under the Surveillance Accountability Act, each agency would decide whether its own data collection requires a warrant under section 3119, with no independent review when it decides none is required.
findings.S22.plain: Section 3119, as the Surveillance Accountability Act would add it, requires a warrant from a neutral magistrate for a search. The agency that wants the data would decide in the first instance whether its conduct is a search and whether an exception for consent, public information or exigent circumstances applies. A judge would review the matter only if the agency concluded that a warrant was needed. The bill requires no report, audit or notice covering the cases in which the agency concluded that it was not.
findings.S22.tech: The warrant requirement supplies an independent check for searches that reach a court. The decisions that determine whether a matter reaches a court are left to the investigating agency, which benefits from a narrow reading of "search" and a broad reading of the exceptions in section 3119(b). The cause of action in section 1979A depends on the person searched learning of the search, and the bill has no notice requirement.
findings.S22.use: An agency could classify a data acquisition as outside section 3119, or as within the consent or exigent circumstances exception, and no court, inspector general or member of the public would be told of that decision.
findings.S22.am.S22a.label: Yearly audit of decisions not to seek a warrant
findings.S22.am.S22a.cost: A yearly audit by each agency's Inspector General would add cost, and a public summary would have to be written so that it does not expose investigative methods. Inspectors general are appointed within the executive branch, so an audit is less independent than review by a court.
conflicts.0.claim: Under the Surveillance Accountability Act, the agency that wants a person's data would decide whether its own collection of that data requires a warrant.
conflicts.0.detail: Each agency would decide whether its own acquisition of data is a search under section 3119 and whether an exception applies. A judge would review a search only when the agency concluded that a warrant was needed and applied for one. The bill requires no report or audit of the cases in which the agency concluded that no warrant was needed.
conflicts.1.who: Each agency that conducts a search
conflicts.1.claim: Under the Surveillance Accountability Act, the agency conducting a search would decide whether an emergency or consent excuses that search from the warrant requirement.
conflicts.1.detail: Exigent circumstances and consent are two of the exceptions in section 3119(b). The agency that benefits from an exception would decide whether it applies, and the bill requires no review after the agency relies on one.
conf_note: No conflicts involving named individuals have been researched for this bill, which is not law and assigns no duty to a named official.
